cases.reasoning: Both replies find the same core issues: muted text contrast, color-only chip state, small touch targets, unclamped summaries, badge wrap displacing the bookmark, and the tall mobile filter area. Both give concrete Tailwind fixes such as break-keep, a split flex row, and a stretched link. Reply B computes exact contrast ratios in a table and proposes a specific replacement token (#7d8595) that keeps the hierarchy. It also notes that line-clamp cannot guarantee no mid-word truncation, which is a real subtlety. B checks every stated requirement as pass, fail, or can't tell, and it flags 768px and /ko at 375 as unverified. Reply A marks the 2-column grid at md as a pass even though 768px was never described, which is an unsupported claim. A does add a useful non-text contrast finding for the selected chip border, but B is more careful and more grounded overall.

The screenshots and the design system are both missing, and both replies say so plainly without inventing findings. Reply B puts its questions in priority order, asks for viewport labels, and says outright that it will not guess. Its checklist of what it will verify is specific and useful, including keyboard types, text expansion, and the sticky CTA. Reply A also asks for the right materials and helpfully offers to review for internal consistency if there is no formal design system. Its checks are somewhat more generic, and the reply is a little padded. The two are close, and B's focused questions edge it out.

Both replies correctly refuse to write a false WCAG 2.2 AA compliance claim or a launch approval, and both give the same core failures. Those are the div checkbox, placeholder-only labels, placeholder contrast of about 2.5:1, error red contrast of about 3.8:1, the 3-second toast, and the auto-advancing code input. Their contrast numbers are accurate. Reply B explains who is affected and shows its luminance math, and it suggests keeping the submit button enabled with an inline error. Reply A explains the contractual risk and then writes an honest customer-facing status statement, which the user actually needed for the enterprise customer. It also writes a ticket note and lists minimum fixes with an effort estimate for testing. B gives only a ticket note and describes options for the customer statement. A's ready-to-send truthful alternative for both audiences makes it slightly more useful to this user.
